newsitem.title: KENYA: High interest rates worry Kenyan central bank.
newsitem.headline: High interest rates worry Kenyan central bank.

text.p: Governor Micah Cheserem of the Central Bank of Kenya on Wednesday lamented high prevailing interest rates in Kenya and said he saw no justification for them.
"The level of interest rates amounts to killing the goose that lays the golden egg," Cheserem told a business gathering, adding that the rates had become a stumbling point to investment in Kenya.
Cheserem blamed commercial banks for the high interest rates and said he saw absolutely no justification for the phenomenon.
Commercial banks base lending rates lie in the 25 percent to 35 percent range. Mortgage rates stand at around 30 percent.
Interest rates are at the heart of Kenya's economic debate. There is no sign that the rates will ease in the near-term.
Commercial banks say they levy high rates because their benchmark is the main 91-day category of treasury bills whose rates have been in the 20-24 percent range over the last year.
They add that if the government significantly reduced its borrowing, it would not have to pay high interest on treasury bills and the market would accordingly adjust.

But the central bank says treasury bill investment is dominated by commercial banks and they persistently bid very high levels of interest rates so that if the government wants to sell its bills it would have to accept current high rates.
Alexander Kaminchia, Executive Chairman at leading retail bankers Kenya Commercial Bank , said "interest rates remain stubborn at high levels which adversely affect lending."
In KCB's annual report, Kaminchia suggested that interest rates would remain high because fundamentals had not adjusted.
Financial analysts say with underlying inflation firmly in the single digit range, they fail to understand why interest rates are as high as 35 percent.

Finance professor Joseph Kimura, of the independent Institute of Policy Analysis and Research, told Reuters high interest rates tended to generate even higher interest rates in subsequent periods as prices of commodities were adjusted upwards to reflect the high cost of borrowing.
"This in turns leads to higher rates of inflation and the cycle begins all over again," Kimura added.
Three-month annualised inflation eased to 32.5 percent in April from 35.6 in March, while the month-on-month annualised rate rose to 16.1 percent in April from 15.6 percent in March.
